catalog_quote: Forster 1963 pp.19-20: "2. Contrastive features of pitch, stress, and length occur on polysyllabic roots of Dibabawon. Any of these features may be modified by intonation... 2.1 On utterances having unmodified statement intonation, high pitch occurs regularly on the penultimate syllable. This is true in isolated or "list" words and also in longer utterances. ... 2.2 Primary stress falls on the final or penultimate syllable of a polysyllabic word. Since speakers of American English tend to "hear" louder stress on any syllable which carries relatively higher pitch, the fact that high pitch consistently occurs on the penultimate syllable of any utterance having unmodified statement intonation gives the impression that primary stress always occurs there also. new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Dibabawon Manobo has an empty rule and no existing statements; this source supplies a placement (predictable penultimate high pitch, non-contrastive), so it adds a rule rather than agreeing or contradicting. Caveat: the statement is about pitch in 'a normal statement' and may be intonational rather than a word-stress rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Prominence (realised as high pitch) is predictable, not contrastive, and falls on the penultimate syllable; the phoneme chart on pp. v–vi lists no stress or pitch phoneme and the orthography does not mark it. The sentence is phrased as 'the penultimate syllable of a normal statement', so it does not itself separate word-level penultimate prominence from a phrase-final intonation peak; the fuller description is deferred to Forster 1963 (Dibabawon phonemes and syllable structure), which was not opened.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; dialect notes concern segments only (Monkayo and eastern dialects replace h with glottal stop; western dialect replaces the pepet vowel with a in vowel sequences)
new_statements.identity_note: Forster & Barnard 1987 note dialect differences in segments only (Monkayo dialect and the eastern dialect: h replaced by glottal stop; western dialect: pepet vowel replaced by a in vowel sequences); the pitch statement is given for the language as a whole, not for one dialect. The listed archive.org item rosettaproject_ilk_phon-1 is about Ilongot (Kakiduge:n Bugkalut), not Dibabawon Manobo. Two files already in our check folder from an earlier reading (ijllt_manobo_davao.*, usep2025_obo_manobo.*) concern Manobo of Davao Occidental and Obo/Kinamiging Manobo, not Dibabawon, and were not used.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between sources, because only one usable statement was found. The one caveat is internal to that statement: Forster & Barnard 1987 (p. vi) say high pitch is predictable on 'the penultimate syllable of a normal statement', which is compatible with word-level penultimate prominence (the reading given here, low confidence) but could equally describe a phrase-final intonation peak; the extract does not use the word 'stress' and defers the full account to Forster 1963, which was not opened. The listed Reid 1971 entry could not be read (wrong item at the listed URL; full scan borrow-only), so it neither confirms nor contradicts.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation from Forster 1963 pp.19-20 is verbatim in the PDF we hold/text layer and on the held p.20 page image; the secondary-stress and p.24-25 statements are also there. (2) The classification rests on a 1963 primary phonology article by the language's principal fieldworker; it explicitly distinguishes contrastive word stress (final ~ penult, penult more frequent, minimal pair 'sa.kit/sa.'kit) from predictable utterance-penult high pitch, which is exactly the distinction the record uses to overrule the earlier phrase-level screen based on the 1987 texts intro. Glottolog (16 refs, none a grammar; Forster 1963 the only phonology), SIL archives (11 items, same picture) and a web search show no later grammar, phonology, dissertation or instrumental study of Dibabawon; the 1987 SIL texts volume itself refers readers to Forster 1963.
